title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's your Friday research digest across the five tracked topics. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from sources like PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH/PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the AASM — citations are linked as chips below each section. This is informational only, not medical advice.

sections.body:
The longevity field's biggest recent signal is still **rapamycin (an mTOR inhibitor)** — and this year the story became more concrete for women specifically.

- The **PEARL trial** (48-week, decentralized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; NCT04488601) is the longest RCT of intermittent low-dose rapamycin in healthy adults aged 50–85. Its primary endpoint — **visceral fat — did *not* change**, and blood biomarkers stayed in normal ranges. But **women on 10 mg/week gained significant lean tissue mass** (roughly ~5% vs. baseline by week 48) and reported **less pain**; the 5 mg group reported better general health. Adverse events matched placebo, so weekly low-dose use looks **relatively safe** over a year.
- A caveat the authors flagged: the **compounded rapamycin** they used absorbed only about a third as well as commercial sirolimus, so real-world effects at these doses could differ. Benefits were **modest and sex-specific**.
- On **senolytics**, a phase 2 trial of **dasatinib + quercetin (D+Q)** in 60 postmenopausal women (NCT04313634) **missed its primary bone-resorption endpoint**, with only exploratory hints of benefit in women carrying a higher senescent-cell burden. Translation: senolytic hype still runs ahead of the human data.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, treat single-supplement "longevity" claims skeptically, and expect **modest** effects so far.

sections.body:
The 2026 evidence base keeps pointing the same way: HIIT is a **time-efficient cardio booster** for women — but not a one-stop program.

- A **2026 systematic review & meta-analysis** (19 RCTs, PubMed/Web of Science/Scopus through Nov 2025) in middle-aged and older women found HIIT **significantly improves VO2max** (SMD = 1.20, 95% CI 0.86–1.54) with **high certainty** of evidence, consistent across age, body-mass status, and program length. Walking ability improved borderline-significantly.
- The same review found **no significant gain in muscle strength** from HIIT alone. The authors explicitly conclude HIIT should sit inside a **multimodal program with resistance and balance work** — not replace it.
- Reassuring on fairness of adaptation: a meta-analysis across 28 trials (462 women, 503 men) found **no sex differences** in VO2max gains (women g = 0.57; men g = 0.57), with well-trained women even out-gaining men on peak power output.
- In **recreationally active younger women** (2025 *Scientific Reports* meta-analysis), HIIT significantly improved cardiorespiratory fitness and **reduced body-fat percentage**.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio gains for women of all training levels; **add resistance training** for strength and lean mass, and progress volume gradually.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI), and a cluster of 2026 RCTs sharpens the how-to.

- **Supervision matters.** A **2026 RCT** (60 women, *Indonesian Journal of Urology*) directly compared supervised vs. unsupervised home PFMT: the **supervised group** cut pad-test leakage from 22.9 g to **3.2 g** (p < 0.001) and got **66.7% to Oxford grade 4–5** strength vs. just 13.3% unsupervised. Unsupervised training still helps *if* adherence is good.
- A **2026 nurse-led RCT** (120 postmenopausal women) delivering a structured **12-week** program produced large drops in incontinence severity (ICIQ-UI SF 7.7 vs. 13.7; Cohen's d = 1.67) that were **sustained at 6 months**, and worked across stress, mixed, and urge subtypes.
- **Add-ons can boost results:** combining Kegels with **EMSELLA electromagnetic stimulation** beat stimulation alone, and a double-blind RCT found **vaginal androgen cream + PFMT** improved remission rates over PFMT + placebo in postmenopausal women.

Key point: **technique, supervision, and consistency** matter more than raw rep count. Confirm correct activation with a clinician or biofeedback.

sections.body:
The most relevant recent work for **HER2-positive, TP53/p53-mutated** breast cancer is a mechanistic study (PubMed/PMC, 2025) explaining why these "co-mutated" tumors resist standard HER2 therapy — and how to exploit that weakness.

- Researchers bred **HER2 V777L** mice with **TP53 mutant alleles (R172H and truncating fl/fl)**. The TP53 mutations **accelerated tumor growth** and made tumors **resistant to neratinib alone** — but the tumors stayed **sensitive to exatecan**, the topoisomerase-I (TOP1) inhibitor payload inside **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd / Enhertu)**.
- Mechanism: mutant-p53 tumors showed **increased histone acetylation, more open chromatin, and hyper-transcription of DNA-repair genes**, pushing cells into G2/M arrest and apoptosis when hit with TOP1 inhibitors. Combining **neratinib + T-DXd** was highly effective preclinically.
- Clinical status update: the human **phase 1 trial** of this combination (NCI ETCTN 10495, **NCT05372614**) reached its primary completion (Sept 2025) and is currently listed on ClinicalTrials.gov as **SUSPENDED for correlative sample analysis**, with an estimated completion in early 2027.

Important framing: this is **early, investigational** evidence. "Alternative" here should mean *evidence-based options discussed with an oncologist* — not a substitute for standard care. p53 itself remains largely **undruggable**, with no approved p53-targeted therapy yet.

sections.body:
The newest guidance continues to put **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements** for chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep.

- A **2026 AASM clinical practice guideline** on *combination* therapy (published with a systematic review and meta-analysis in the *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*) issued two conditional recommendations: combining CBT-I with medication is better than **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone**. **CBT-I stays first-line.**
- The underlying **meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (Buysse et al., 2026)** found a clear asymmetry: **adding CBT-I to an existing medication** meaningfully improved insomnia severity, sleep efficiency, sleep-onset latency, and wake-after-sleep-onset — while **adding medication to CBT-I cleared no clinically meaningful threshold** and was associated with slightly **worse depression scores**.
- On supplements/drugs: **prolonged-release melatonin** shows only **modest** benefit, mostly in adults **over 55** or mild insomnia — not a first-line fix; evidence for **magnesium** is limited. Newer **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** are better tolerated than Z-drugs but have less long-term data.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Use the bed **only for sleep**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If problems persist beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out sleep apnea and consider **CBT-I** (including digital CBT-I).
